# SIXTOM — full content

> everyone's building. nothing's better. the enablement engagement, for teams already building with AI: two weeks, one team. by day 10 one process that lived in people's heads is written down, running, and owned by a named person on your team, or the rest is free. $15,000 fixed. one team a month.

## thesis

building got cheap. deciding didn't.

anyone on your team can build a tool in an afternoon now. so they do. nobody decides which ones should exist. every month it stays like this has a price: the pile: tools nobody asked for, kept alive by whoever made them. the queue: one person reviews everything, or nobody reviews anything. the date: the steps live in three heads and a chat thread, so it slips. that part is fixable in two weeks.

## the offer — one engagement, everything in it

two weeks with your team, on the one process that keeps running late. you pick it on the first call. everything in the engagement, and what it'd cost you piecemeal:

### the diagnosis

- the inventory — everything your team has built, who uses it, what's quietly broken — $1,500
- one metric, one definition — the number everyone argues about gets a single source of truth — $3,000

### the process

- written down — one process, step by step, with an owner and a yes or no on each step — core
- runnable — the steps your team repeats every week become something anyone can run by asking — $4,000
- the red light — when a step is late, its owner hears that day. so does everyone waiting on it — $1,000

### the guardrails

- permissions + review gate — nothing reaches production without review, and the person who knows the work reviews it — $3,000
- repo rules — one branch per tool, hooks, shared instructions. a 45,000-line PR can't happen — $2,500
- access, trimmed — who needs to be in the repo and the systems, and who never did. customer data comes off laptops — $2,000

### the people

- hands-on onboarding — the people who run the process, set up. by the tenth person it takes one sitting — $4,000
- the tracing-paper session — git and review, explained so it sticks for people who never wanted to learn git — $1,500
- the leadership session — the people at the top use it first, so the team follows — $2,000

### the close (bonuses land by day 30)

- running by day 10 — you own 100% of it — included
- day-30 check-in — what stuck, what didn't — $500
- the runbook + Loom library — so the next hire onboards without me — $1,500
- the 90-day map — the next three things worth doing, in order. and the ones to buy instead of build — $1,500

**total value: $28,000+. you pay: $15,000 fixed. half up front, half on day 10.**

a consultancy quotes six figures and delivers a deck. a workshop is half a day and a recording nobody watches. this is two weeks, and something running when i leave.

## the guarantee

your person runs it by day 10, or the rest is free.

and there's a floor under it: day 5, we both look at it. if we can both see it won't be running in scope, we stop there. you keep everything we built and pay only for the time used. the risk is mine to carry, not yours.

## the teardown

$1,500, credited in full against the engagement if you book one within 30 days. i look at how your team works today: the tools, the automations, the numbers people argue about. you get a 10-minute Loom and a written list of what's stuck and what i'd fix first. you keep it whether or not we work together, and i'll tell you if you don't need me. to start one, join the waitlist and reply to the email.

## proof — inside a consumer brand

since july i've run 22 onboarding sessions across ops, finance, marketing, wholesale and creative. into a shared repo, behind a review gate. none of them were hired to write code. by the tenth session, setup took one sitting. three glue chains are code now. one finance analyst shipped dashboards fast enough that their lead asked them to slow down.

what broke when it worked. i became the review queue. everything waited on me. thousands of tests, good ones. most never needed to exist. i built tools faster than i asked who would use them. the process stayed in people's heads. nobody can run that. so the first thing we make now is a document. the build comes second, and it's smaller.

before this, the craft: a solo therapy practice rebuilt in 4h43m. mobile load 8.3s → 2.9s. pageviews up 185%. same hands.

## who it's for

this is for you if: your team is building. you can't tell what it adds up to · the people building aren't engineers · a date slipped and nobody saw it coming · you'd rather your people own it than rent a consultancy.

not yet if: nobody on your team has shipped anything yet. start with the teardown · it's just you. no team yet · you want a workshop and a recording · you want it done for you, with nobody on your side learning.

## how the two weeks go

- day 0: a 30-minute call. we pick the person and the process.
- week 1: we write it down together, step by step, then make each step runnable. a daily Loom so leadership watches it happen.
- day 5 · scope check: if it won't be running in scope, we stop here. you keep what we built.
- week 2: the red light goes on. the guardrails go in. the people who run it get set up. one session with leadership.
- day 10: running. your person owns it. (or the rest is free.)
- day 30: check-in. what stuck, what didn't.

## FAQ

**what does sixtom do?**

your team is building with AI and the work isn't getting better. in two weeks, one process that lived in people's heads is written down, runs without anyone chasing it, and goes red the day a step is late. a named person on your team owns it, and the guardrails hold as more people build. you own all of it.

**how much does it cost?**

$15,000 fixed. half up front, half on day 10. that buys everything itemized on the home page, over $28,000 of work. the price is the same for everyone.

**what's the guarantee?**

your person is running the process by day 10, or you don't pay the second half. there's a floor under it too: at the day-5 scope check, if we can both see it won't be running in scope, we stop. you keep everything built and pay only for the time used.

**what's the teardown?**

$1,500, credited in full against the engagement if you book one within 30 days. i look at how your team works today: the tools, the automations, the numbers people argue about. you get a 10-minute Loom and a written list of what's stuck and what i'd fix first. you keep it whether or not we work together, and i'll tell you if you don't need me. to start one, join the waitlist and reply to the email.

**how long does it take?**

two weeks. running by day 10. one team a month, by appointment.

**does my team need to be technical?**

no. the people i onboard work in ops, finance, marketing and wholesale. none of them were hired to write code. they need a setup that works, a review gate, and someone to explain git with tracing paper.

**how many clients do you take?**

one team a month, by appointment. that's the whole model. you get my full attention, not a queue. when the seat's taken, the waitlist is open.

**what happens after the two weeks?**

you own everything: the process, the repo, the runbook. there's a day-30 check-in to see what stuck. if you want me back for the next process, we talk then.

**who's behind sixtom?**

Salvatore (Sam) D'Angelo, leads engineering and AI at a consumer brand (multi-million visitors a month), formerly at Rhone. sixtom is the solo practice.

**is it remote?**

yes. working sessions over video, a daily Loom, and everything lands in your repo. no standups.

## case study — garden party

a 1:1 port of threesam.com from Next.js to SvelteKit. five hours of build time. bundle size dropped 40%. every Lighthouse score went up. full writeup at https://sixtom.com/log/garden-party.

the premise: take a 30-route personal site (canvas sketches, video heroes, real-time data feeds, the works) and port it to SvelteKit — the framework i prefer and ship freelance, just never at the day job. same routes, same sketches, same aesthetic — different runtime. two questions answered honestly: is a 1:1 port across frameworks possible, and is it worth it?
